inline.s: [Delimited birth-and-death] Beings within the three realms and the six paths, whose lifespans are all limited and whose bodies are all of distinct kinds, because of the good and evil karma they have attracted—their birth-and-death is therefore called “delimited birth-and-death.” One who has ended delimited birth-and-death escapes the wheel of rebirth and leaves the three realms. [Transformational birth-and-death] The sages of the Three Vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and ended delimited birth-and-death, gradually extinguish deluded thought and gradually increase their realization as they cultivate the path. This migration of delusion and awakening differs in every period; the passage from the earlier period into the later is exactly like one round of birth-and-death, and its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, inconceivable—hence it is called “transformational birth-and-death.” One who has ended transformational birth-and-death perfectly realizes the Buddha fruit.
The true nature of all dharmas is this: all dharmas are illusory, fundamentally not a single thing exists. In
fascicle ten of the Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sutra
, the Buddha says:
“All dharmas are like illusion, like a dream, like an echo, like a shadow, like a flame.”

In the Sutra of Holding the World, the Buddha says: “Know that all dharmas are empty, like illusion without reality, without any root.” In the Sutra Spoken by the Buddha for King Prasenajit on the Royal Law, the Buddha says:

“All dharmas are empty in substance and nature, impermanent, perishing and destroyed. Suppose a man in the night, in a dream, sees fine parks and gardens, mountains and rivers, people and crowds, dense forests and clear springs, halls, houses and pavilions—all delightful. When he wakes up
(to wake from sleep; here the ‘jue’ of ‘shuijue’ means to awaken)
, he sees not one thing.”
(For the true nature of all dharmas, see in detail
The True Nature of All Dharmas
[Dream and awakening] To wake from a dream. Master Taixu said:
“The mind within a dream is the mind of an ordinary being; the mind that knows it dreams within the dream is the mind of a bodhisattva; the mind that has awakened from the dream is the Buddha-mind.”
(An Outline of the Contemplation of Consciousness-Only)
The true nature of all dharmas is the supreme truth. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false. Where they cease—that is called the real, that is called the true nature, that is called the dharma realm, that is called ultimate knowledge, that is called the supreme truth, that is called supreme emptiness.”
(Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
fascicle forty.)
The true nature of all dharmas is the dharma-seal of the Mahāyāna sutras—the seal of true nature. Master Zhiyi says in the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra,
fascicle eight:

“Among the Lesser Vehicle sutras, those sealed by the three seals of impermanence, non-self and nirvāṇa are spoken by the Buddha, and cultivating them one attains the path. Without the three dharma-seals, they are the words of Māra. The Mahāyāna sutras have only one dharma-seal, called the true nature of all dharmas; they are called sutras of definitive meaning and can lead to the great path. Without the seal of true nature, they are the words of Māra.”
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This means that all marks are illusions. This includes mountains, rivers and the great earth, the sun, moon and stars, birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, living beings and all Buddhas—all are illusions. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Within it, the buddha-worlds of a hundred thousand koṭis of asamkhyeya—inexpressible—Ganges-sands, are like a flower in the sky, arising and perishing in confusion.” “There is fundamentally no bodhi and no nirvāṇa, no attaining Buddhahood and no not attaining Buddhahood, no deluded rebirth and no non-rebirth.” “Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike marks of a flower in the sky.”

[Asamkhyeya] Rendered into Chinese as ‘countless,’ meaning so many that no number can calculate them. [Flower in the sky] In the Buddhadharma this is often used to illustrate illusion. A ‘flower in the sky’ is a flower in empty space. One with diseased eyes sees flowers in empty space, yet empty space originally has no flowers—it is only the illusion of the diseased eye. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Falsely taking the four great elements as one’s own body, and the shadows of the six dusts as the marks of one’s own mind—like a diseased eye seeing flowers in the sky, and a second moon.”
The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp says:
“With one film over the eye, flowers in the sky fall in confusion.”

In the dream-illusion of “all that has marks is false and illusory” there are two utterly different roads: one is to use illusion to leave illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream is awakened—this is the path of bodhi; the other is to use illusion to enter illusion, turning through birth-and-death—this is the road of rebirth that living beings have walked since beginningless kalpas. The Diamond Sutra arms us with diamond prajñā to awaken to and break through illusion, to be deluded and inverted no more, and to walk the great path of bodhi that is “using illusion to leave illusion, until illusion is exhausted and the dream is awakened.” This sutra says:

“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “No mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of living beings, no mark of a life-span.” “No mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.” “Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.” “Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
The Sutra of the Inconceivable State of the Tathāgata says:
“All Tathāgatas rely on this samādhi to accomplish immeasurable great awesome spiritual power, and even to realize and enter the emptiness of all dharmas
(all dharmas are illusions)

, and can therefore manifest all kinds of sovereign matters in all buddha-lands of the ten directions. Suppose a man dreams of all sorts of transformed things, and when he wakes, all he saw is gone. Ordinary beings are likewise:
because of the dream of ignorance
they falsely give rise to the notion of a real substance in regard to all dharmas. The Buddhas, having awakened
(the Buddhas have woken from the dream of ignorance)

, are attached to nothing; therefore in all worlds of the ten directions they can, in a single thought, manifest immeasurable buddha-works, sovereign and unobstructed, benefiting and bringing to accomplishment all living beings, causing them all to awaken and enter the immeasurable and profound wondrous gate of liberation.”

What does the Diamond Sutra teach? The Diamond Sutra teaches the true nature of all dharmas—that all dharmas are illusory—causing living beings to break delusion and eliminate attachment and thereby attain liberation. But living beings’ two attachments, to self and to dharmas, are deep-rooted and hard to believe; therefore the World-Honored One and Subhūti, in the form of dialogue, break through doubt layer upon layer, causing Subhūti and we living beings to remove doubt and give rise to faith, so that our inherent wisdom may appear. Examined thus, living beings and Buddhas are equal and the two attachments both perish—this is the essential key to leaving illusion and becoming Buddha. (For the true nature of all dharmas, see in detail
The True Nature of All Dharmas

Zong is the essential principle; qu is the direction toward which it tends. Purpose and direction is the method of cultivation that carries the essential principle through—how to practice in accordance with the sutra’s substance, the so-called seeking the principle and returning to its direction. The purpose and direction of this sutra is: leaving marks—leaving the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings, the mark of a life-span, the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas. Relying on the wondrous principle of the true nature of all dharmas, one leaves marks and does not abide, in order to break delusion and eliminate attachment. The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Leaving marks, one is without marks; without marks, one does not abide; not abiding, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the Buddha says:

“Good sons! Those newly learned bodhisattvas and living beings of the final age who wish to seek the Tathāgata’s pure and perfect enlightenment mind should abide in right mindfulness and keep far from all illusions.”

[Mark of self] Falsely clinging to the body and mind of the five aggregates as truly existent, and taking them as “I” and giving rise to mind—for example, gain and loss, adversity and favorable conditions, honor and disgrace, and so on. [Mark of person] Falsely clinging to the other party, to other people, as truly existent and giving rise to mind—for example, like and dislike, right and wrong, high and low, and so on. [Mark of living beings] Here “living beings” means groups of people—for example, groups distinguished by closeness and distance, likes and dislikes, friend and enemy, age, sex, workplace, region, race, skin color, nation, and so on. The mark of living beings is falsely clinging to these groups as truly existent and giving rise to discriminating mind. [Mark of a life-span] Falsely clinging to lifespan as truly existent and calculating its length. What deluded living beings care about most is nothing other than lifespan; therefore the mark of a life-span is separated out from the mark of self and set up as a separate item. [Mark of dharmas] Falsely clinging to all dharmas (including the dharmas of the path) as truly existent. [Dharmas of the path] The dharmas of cultivating the path, that is, the dharmas for ending birth-and-death and realizing nirvāṇa. [Mark of non-dharmas] Denying all dharmas (including the dharmas of the path), falsely clinging to all dharmas as non-existent and sinking into stubborn emptiness
When the World-Honored One attained the path, his very first words were:
“Wondrous! Wondrous! All living beings on the great earth are fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks, but because of deluded thought and attachment they cannot realize them.”
Therefore, dispelling deluded thought and attachment is the way to Buddhahood. How is it dispelled? By leaving marks! Hence section fourteen of this sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
The so-called leaving of marks is simply not clinging to marks—knowing that marks are illusion, not being deluded by marks, not being turned by marks. This sutra says:
“Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.” “If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathāgata.”

[Clinging to marks] Clinging to marks is taking marks as real; then desire arises and thoughts arise, and one runs after desire and thought. Thus one creates karma, and thus one turns through birth-and-death. [Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness] Not clinging to marks as real, and not being moved by them.
In the fifth section, “Truly Seeing Through the Principle,” the Buddha says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.”

This means that all marks are illusions; yet living beings, since beginningless time, have taken illusions as real, so deluded thought and attachment never cease, and they are seduced and coerced by them—thus they create karma, thus they receive retribution, thus they turn through birth-and-death and sink into the sea of suffering. Now, to attain liberation and return to the source, one must no longer be deluded by illusions and must not be turned by marks; this requires leaving marks and dispelling deluded thought and attachment.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“When the preceding thought is deluded
(clinging to marks—being turned by marks)
, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought awakens
(not grasping at marks—leaving marks)
, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves objects, that is bodhi.”
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“Seeing illusion, one is immediately free of it, without applying expedients; leaving illusion, one is immediately awakened, with no gradual stages.”
Therefore one should
“not grasp at marks, but be unmoving in suchness.”
(section thirty-two of this sutra)
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is called Chan concentration? Externally leaving marks is Chan; inwardly not being confused is concentration. If outwardly one clings to marks, the inner mind is confused; if outwardly one leaves marks, the mind is not confused. The intrinsic nature is itself pure and itself still; it is only because one sees objects and thinks of objects that it is confused. If one sees all objects and the mind is not confused, that is true concentration.”

Aware of the present thought, one enters the state without thought—this is leaving marks; this is doing the work of leaving marks at the very place where thought arises and the mind stirs. Inwardly not turned by thoughts, outwardly not dragged by objects—in the vast wind of circumstances, one is one’s own master.
Section fourteen of this sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
This is the meaning of “Diamond Prajñāpāramitā” in the sutra’s title: by wondrous diamond wisdom, leaving marks and becoming Buddha. In section thirteen, the Buddha says:
“This sutra is named the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā. By this name you should uphold it.”
Diamond prajñā is the great wisdom that, seeing marks, can leave them.
Section eight says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.”
Section fourteen says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
Therefore the way to Buddhahood is what this sutra repeatedly speaks of:
leaving marks

In leaving marks one must cultivate compassion and emptiness together, cultivating the contemplation of compassion while cultivating emptiness, for only thus can one be unattached to both emptiness and existence and leave marks thoroughly and ultimately. If one cultivates emptiness alone, though one may not be attached to existence, one will become attached to emptiness. The sutra says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”

Leaving all marks means not only leaving the marks of existence but also leaving the marks of emptiness; in the end even the mark of leaving marks must be left, until there is nothing left to leave—only then is it ultimate and perfect, only then is the Buddha’s path accomplished. Therefore this sutra says:

“All living beings of whatever kind—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with thought, without thought, or neither with thought nor without thought—I cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without residue and be liberated. And thus immeasurable, countless, boundless living beings are liberated, yet in truth no living being attains liberation. Why? Subhūti! If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span, he is not a bodhisattva.”
This is compassion and emptiness cultivated together, unattached to both emptiness and existence.
In leaving marks, one must first concretely put non-abiding into practice.

Non-abiding is simply not clinging to marks. That is, in regard to the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings, the mark of a life-span, the mark of dharmas and the mark of non-dharmas, there is nothing to abide in (not falsely clinging to them as real). The Precious Mirror of the Pure Land School says:
“Leaving marks, one is without marks; without marks, one does not abide; not abiding, one enters the Buddha’s realm. This is the supreme, true, great bodhisattva path.”
In this sutra, passages on leaving marks and non-abiding are found everywhere. For example:
Section three says:
“If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span, he is not a bodhisattva.”
This means a bodhisattva must leave the four marks.
Section four says:
“If a bodhisattva gives without abiding in marks, his merit is inconceivable.”
This means giving must leave marks.
Section six says:

“Hearing these passages, even a single thought of pure faith arises—Subhūti! The Tathāgata fully knows and fully sees that such living beings attain such immeasurable merit. Why? Because such living beings no longer have the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings or the mark of a life-span; they have no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas.”
Section seven says:
“All sages and saints are distinguished through the unconditioned dharma.”

The unconditioned dharma is leaving marks. This passage says: all sages and saints, because of the differing depth of their leaving of marks, have the distinction of forty-two stages. These forty-two stages are: the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment. Among them, wondrous enlightenment is Buddhahood. Therefore an ancient worthy said:
“Only exhaust the ordinary feelings
(one need only cut off all ordinary feelings)
—there is no other sagely understanding.”

[Wise and noble] A bodhisattva’s cultivation has fifty-two stages: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment—wondrous enlightenment being Buddhahood. Among them, the ten abidings, the ten practices and the ten dedications are the wise (called the three stages of the wise), while the ten grounds, equal enlightenment and wondrous enlightenment are the noble.
Section ten says:

“Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; they should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.”
This speaks of leaving the marks of dust-objects: not giving rise to mind abiding in dust-objects, and even when mind arises, not abiding in dust-objects.
Section fourteen says:
“A bodhisattva should leave all marks and give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment.”
This means: on the path of bodhi, from the very beginning, at the moment of giving rise to the mind, one must leave marks.
In section seventeen, Subhūti asks again:
“World-Honored One! When good men and good women give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”
The Buddha answers:

“Good men and good women who give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment should thus give rise to the mind: I should liberate all living beings, and when all living beings have been liberated, in truth not one living being has been liberated.”
Therefore the answer to “How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?” is: leaving marks, not abiding, and liberating living beings.
Section twenty-three says:
“With no self, no person, no living beings and no life-span, cultivating all wholesome dharmas, one attains supreme perfect enlightenment.”
This means: leaving the four marks and cultivating any wholesome dharma whatsoever, one realizes the Buddha fruit. From this one sees how important leaving marks is!

(This passage means that the key to realizing supreme perfect enlightenment is being without the four marks, and not what kind of wholesome dharma one cultivates. Wholesome dharmas cultivated without the four marks are the unconditioned dharma. Here the World-Honored One reveals to us the universal principle for realizing supreme perfect enlightenment; from this we also know how pivotal and how important it is to leave the four marks!)
At the end of this sutra, the World-Honored One says:
“Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

This echoes what the World-Honored One displayed at the very beginning of the sutra—putting on his robe, begging for food, washing his feet and spreading his seat—and it runs through the whole sutra. This is leaving marks, not being turned by circumstances, not being dragged by thoughts, unmoving in suchness. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“What is called Chan concentration? Externally leaving marks is Chan; inwardly not being confused is concentration. If outwardly one clings to marks, the inner mind is confused; if outwardly one leaves marks, the mind is not confused. The intrinsic nature is itself pure and itself still; it is only because one sees objects and thinks of objects that it is confused. If one sees all objects and the mind is not confused, that is true concentration.”
Therefore the key to Chan concentration is leaving marks.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sutra,
fascicle one,
the Chapter on Learning the Contemplations, says:
“Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should take non-attachment as their expedient means and perfect prajñāpāramitā, because the nature and marks of all dharmas cannot be grasped.”
“Non-attachment” is not clinging to marks—that is, leaving marks.
This sutra says:
“All that has marks is false and illusory.” “Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

This is the core of upholding the Diamond Sutra—leaving marks. And in the course of learning to leave marks, one should take “stilling deluded thought and breaking the mark of self” as the focus and the point of entry.

Purpose and direction is the cause; benefit is the fruit. This sutra cultivates both merit and wisdom, and its benefits are: breaking delusion and eliminating attachment, producing merit and extinguishing offenses, dissolving karma and escaping suffering, and realizing bodhi. The sutra says a great deal about this, and I shall not enumerate it here; when studying the sutra text, one should match each point one by one.

The character of the teaching” refers to the differing characters of the Buddha’s teaching throughout his life—that is, the features of the various doctrines and their differences. The Buddha taught living beings according to their capacities. Living beings’ faculties are dull or sharp, their obstacles thick or thin; therefore the sutras have teachings that are shallow or deep, gradual or sudden, partial or complete, provisional or ultimate, small or great (Lesser Vehicle, Great Vehicle).

[Partial and complete] Partial and complete. “Partial” means leaning to one side; “complete” means perfectly interfused and unobstructed. [Provisional and ultimate] A teaching suited to a particular time is called “provisional”; a teaching that is ultimate and unchanging is called “ultimate.”

The character of this sutra’s teaching is: the most complete, the most sudden, and the most real of the One Vehicle sutras. “Most complete” means this sutra is the most ultimate and definitive; “most sudden” means this sutra’s teaching does not pass through the various stages but enters directly in a single leap; “most real” means this sutra directly sets forth the true nature of all dharmas; “One Vehicle” means this sutra is the sole teaching that causes people to become Buddha.

[One Vehicle] Also called the Buddha Vehicle—the sole teaching that can cause people to become Buddha. “Vehicle” means a carriage; it is used to illustrate the Buddha’s teaching, because the teaching can carry people to the other shore of nirvāṇa, and so it is called a “vehicle.” [Definitive meaning] The principle set forth is utterly complete, thorough and ultimate.
Question: Why is it said that the Diamond Sutra is the most complete, most sudden and most real One Vehicle sutra?
Answer: The sutra says:
“All Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra”
(section eight);
“the Tathāgata speaks it for those who have set out on the Great Vehicle, and for those who have set out on the Supreme Vehicle”
(section fifteen)—this shows that this sutra is the most complete One Vehicle teaching. The Buddha says:
“Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.”
This speaks of leaving all marks completely and directly (without passing through the various stages) becoming Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch records:
“The Master
(the Fifth Patriarch of Chan, Hongren)
constantly urged monks and laity simply to uphold the Diamond Sutra, and they would thereby see their own nature and directly become Buddha.”
—this shows that this sutra is most sudden. (Section fourteen.) The sutra constantly uses the logical formula “
A
is not
A
, therefore it is called
A”
to demonstrate that all dharmas are illusion, and it also says
“all that has marks is false and illusory”
(section five); both are speaking of the true nature of all dharmas—showing that this sutra is the most real.
[Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin]—
Master Kumārajīva is the translator of this sutra.

Yao Qin”: in history there were three Qin dynasties. One was the state of Qin of the Warring States period, down to the Qin dynasty that unified the realm under the First Emperor. The second Qin dynasty arose in the period of the Five Barbarians and Sixteen Kingdoms, its sovereign being Fu Jian. The third Qin dynasty was founded when Yao Chang, a great general of Fu Jian, killed Fu Jian and set himself up, also calling his state Qin; later generations, to distinguish it from the Qin dynasty of Fu Jian’s time, called it Yao Qin, also known as the Later Qin.

Tripiṭaka”: the sutra-piṭaka, the vinaya-piṭaka and the abhidharma-piṭaka. The sutra-piṭaka is the scriptures spoken by the Buddha; the vinaya-piṭaka is the precepts laid down by the Buddha; the abhidharma-piṭaka is the treatises composed by the Buddha’s disciples. A “Tripiṭaka Master” is a bhikṣu thoroughly versed in all three piṭakas of sutra, vinaya and abhidharma.
Kumārajīva (343–413
CE

) was rendered into Chinese as Tongshou, “Youthful Longevity.” He was by origin a man of Tianzhu (ancient India) and grew up in Kucha (between present-day Kuqa County and Shaya County in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region). Kumarajiva’s father was a man of Tianzhu whose family had for generations served as ministers of state. He avoided the ministership and left home to become a monk, coming to the kingdom of Kucha; when the king of Kucha heard that he had renounced glory to cultivate the path, he revered him deeply and went out beyond the city walls to welcome him and invite him to be the state preceptor. The king’s younger sister was then just twenty, clear and keen in understanding, able to recite what she had read at a single glance, and when the various kingdoms sought her in marriage she refused them all. Seeing Kumarajiva’s father, she wished in her heart to marry him, and the king forced Kumarajiva’s father to take her as wife; thus Kumarajiva was born. At seven, Kumarajiva followed his mother in leaving home, and traveled throughout the Western Regions (the general name for the states west of Yumen and Yangguan in Gansu). He mastered all the texts and was most skilled in the Mahāyāna. In Kucha, when the kings of neighboring states assembled, each time they invited Kumarajiva to preach they would kneel before his seat and have Kumarajiva step on their shoulders to mount the throne. Later his mother realized the fruit of the anāgāmin (the śrāvaka vehicle has four fruits: srota-āpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin and arhat) and said to Kumarajiva: the Mahāyāna teachings can be transmitted to the Middle Kingdom. Kumarajiva replied: if they can be transmitted, I would sacrifice myself to do it.
In the eighteenth year of the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin (382
CE
, when Kumarajiva was
years old), the Qin king Fu Jian sent the great general Lü Guang to lead troops against Yanqi, then to destroy Kucha, and to carry Kumarajiva off to Liangzhou.

Three years later Yao Chang killed Fu Jian, destroyed the Former Qin, and proclaimed himself emperor in Chang’an; Lü Guang then carved out Liangzhou for himself and made himself its ruler, so Kumarajiva remained stranded in Liangzhou for
years. It was not until Yao Xing succeeded to the throne that, in the third year of the Hongshi era, troops were sent west against Liangzhou (401
CE
, when Kumarajiva was

years old); the Liang ruler Lü Long was defeated and surrendered, and the Qin king Yao Xing personally welcomed Kumarajiva into Chang’an, where he lodged in the Western Bright Pavilion of Xiaoyao Garden. He was treated with the courtesy due a state preceptor, and a translation hall of great scale was organized in Chang’an, with Kumarajiva invited to preside over the work of translating the scriptures.

Thereafter, for more than ten years, Master Kumarajiva devoted himself wholeheartedly to translating scriptures and preaching the Dharma. When translating at Caotang Temple, with three thousand monks in all, the Master held the old scriptures in his own hands and deliberated and settled them, and none failed to investigate them minutely and penetrate their profound purport. The assistants in the translation hall were rich in talent, with the names of the Four Worthies, the Eight Talents and the Ten Philosophers; the most famous were Sengzhao, Sengrui, Daorong, Tanying and others. The Master once preached at Caotang Temple, and the Qin king, his court ministers and several thousand śramaṇas listened reverently with solemn countenance. Master Kumarajiva was of the same age as Master Huiyuan of the Eastern Jin, the founding patriarch of the Pure Land school; their kingdoms were not the same (Master Kumarajiva was in the Yao Qin, Master Huiyuan in the Eastern Jin), and they exchanged letters.
Master Kumarajiva translated in all
works,

fascicles. The most important among them are the Large Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, the Smaller Prajñāpāramitā Sutra, the Lotus Sutra of the Wondrous Dharma, the Diamond Sutra, the Vimalakīrti Sutra, the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sutra, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sutra, the Treatise on the Stages of the Ten Grounds, the Madhyamaka Treatise, the Hundred Treatise, the Twelve Gate Treatise, the Satyasiddhi Treatise, and the Vinaya in Ten Recitations. The scriptures he translated were extremely broad in scope, faithful in content and fluent in wording; though some were later retranslated, the new versions could hardly replace them, and they hold epoch-making significance in the history of scripture translation in China.
In the eleventh year of the Hongshi era of the Qin (413
CE

) Master Kumarajiva passed away in Chang’an at the age of seventy. At the end he said: if what I have transmitted is without error, then after my body is burned my tongue will not be scorched or rotted. His remains were cremated in Xiaoyao Garden according to foreign custom; when the fire died and the body was consumed, only the tongue remained unspoiled, like a red lotus.

When annotating sutras and treatises, one usually divides the whole text into paragraphs and sections, which is called textual analysis. Here, the divisions into large sections are called major divisions; the divisions of the major divisions into smaller sections are called minor divisions; and the concise, essential wording that marks the content of each division is called division text. On this basis the reader can learn the concise content and the thread of meaning of the annotation, and can determine the annotator’s general view of that sutra or treatise.

The popular editions of the Diamond Sutra divide the whole sutra into thirty-two sections and give each a title; tradition holds that this was done by Prince Zhaoming, Xiao Tong (son of Emperor Wu of Liang). The purport of this analysis is subtle and wondrous, its chapters are detailed yet concise, and it greatly aids the understanding of the text; hence it has been widely handed down without decline (and there are even remains of a “terrace for dividing the sutra”). This book also follows it. Since the titles of these thirty-two sections are textual analysis and not part of the sutra text, one should not read them when chanting the sutra.

[Terrace for Dividing the Sutra] Located in the Shilian Cave National Forest Park south of Susong County seat, Anhui Province. The Terrace for Dividing the Sutra, also called the Stone of Dividing the Sutra, is five meters high and of oval terrace shape. On it are carved the three large characters “Terrace for Dividing the Sutra,” beside which is written “Erected on the eleventh day of the sixth month of the first year of Jiatai of the Imperial Song.” Tradition holds that Prince Zhaoming of Liang divided the Diamond Sutra into thirty-two sections here, hence the name. The stele was erected in the first year of Jiatai (
CE) to commemorate the seven hundredth anniversary of Prince Zhaoming’s birth.

Judging by its content, this sutra can be divided into two parts. Sections one through sixteen are the first part, and sections seventeen through thirty-two are the second part. The first part teaches how to give rise to the mind, how to liberate living beings, how to subdue delusion and how to cut off delusion; this is breaking the self of person in order to end delimited birth-and-death, but the self of dharmas still remains. Therefore the second part teaches how to break the self of dharmas and end transformational birth-and-death. Hence the World-Honored One says at the very beginning of the second part: “In truth there is no dharma by which one gives rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment.” Then he breaks the self of dharmas layer upon layer, until at the end of the part he says: “How should one expound it for others? Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness. Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and also like lightning—thus should they be contemplated.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and all living beings of the final age should keep far from all illusory and false realms. Because of firmly holding the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like illusion is also to be kept far away from; the keeping far away is itself illusion and is also to be kept far away from; the illusion of keeping far away from keeping far away is also to be kept far away from; when there is nothing left to keep far away from, all illusions are removed. It is like drilling for fire: two sticks rub together, fire comes forth and the sticks are consumed, the ashes fly and the smoke goes out. Cultivating illusion by means of illusion is likewise so; when all illusions are extinguished, one does not fall into annihilation.”

[The two selves] The self of person and the self of dharmas. The self of person is that ordinary beings, not understanding the principle that the five aggregates are falsely compounded, falsely cling to body and mind as “I,” and thereby have the views of self, love of self, pride of self and delusion of self, and so on, forming the affliction obstacle. The self of dharmas is that ordinary beings, not understanding the principle that all dharmas are empty by dependent origination, falsely cling to all dharmas as truly existent, and thereby have discriminating mind, mind of love and hate, mind of becoming Buddha, mind of nirvāṇa, and so on, forming the obstacle of the known.

blocks.text: 3. The Introductory Part, the Main Part and the Circulation Part

inline.s: Traditionally, when annotating a scripture text, one divides it into three great parts: the introductory part, the main part and the circulation part.

The introductory part is the portion that recounts the occasion for the arising of the sutra. Section one of this sutra (Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly) is the introductory part. The introductory part is further divided into two portions: the general introduction and the particular introduction.

The general introduction: this is the introductory account common to all sutras (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was at ...”). For example, the first passage of this sutra (“Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number.”) is the general introduction. The general introduction is also called the introduction that establishes faith, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place and assembly, in order to prove that what is said in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the six accomplishments, the six causes and conditions that accomplish the dharma assembly for preaching the sutra.

The particular introduction: after the general introduction comes the particular introduction, which is where the introductory portions of the various sutras differ from one another. For example, the second passage of this sutra (“At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat and sat down.”) is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is also called the introduction of the arising, because it explains how this dharma assembly came about.
The main part is the portion in which the sutra is properly set forth. Of the whole sutra’s thirty-two sections, from section two through the end of section thirty-one is the main part.

The circulation part is the portion that lists the benefits of upholding this sutra and urges and praises its upholding, recitation and circulation. In this sutra, the last section (Section Thirty-Two: Neither Real nor False) is the circulation part.

blocks.text: Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly

inline.s: The causes and conditions of the dharma assembly” speaks of this sutra, that is, the causes and origin of the Diamond dharma assembly. “Section” corresponds to “chapter.” For example, “Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly” means “Chapter One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly.”

This section (“Section One: The Causes and Conditions of the Dharma Assembly”) is the introductory part. The introductory part is the portion that recounts the occasion for the arising of the sutra. As said before, it is further divided into two portions: the general introduction and the particular introduction.

[Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number.]

This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. At that time the Buddha was in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden in the country of Śrāvastī, together with twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus.

This passage is the general introduction. The general introduction is also called the introduction that establishes faith, because it possesses the six matters of faith, hearing, time, teacher, place and assembly, in order to prove that what is said in the sutra is true and credible. These six matters are also called the six accomplishments, because a sutra can only be accomplished when these six causes and conditions are present.

Let us now take this passage of the sutra as an example to explain the six accomplishments. First, “Thus” is the accomplishment of faith—the Buddha spoke thus. Second, “have I heard” is the accomplishment of hearing—this sutra was heard by me (Ānanda) with my own ears, and was not heard at second or third hand. Third, “at one time” is the accomplishment of time—that is, the time of the dharma assembly for preaching the sutra, when teacher and disciple were united in the way and capacity and teaching met each other. Fourth, “the Buddha” is the accomplishment of the teacher—the master who speaks the Dharma. Fifth, “was in the country of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden” is the accomplishment of place—the place where the Dharma is spoken. Sixth, “together with a great assembly of great bhikṣus, twelve hundred and fifty in number” is the accomplishment of the assembly—the great multitude that hears the sutra. Because it clearly points out that this sutra was personally heard by the compiler of the sutra (Ānanda) as the Buddha spoke it thus, and marks the master who speaks the Dharma as well as the time, place and people of the assembly, causing living beings to know that this sutra is indeed without error and thereby to give rise to faith, it is called the introduction that establishes faith.

[Thus have I heard] This is what I (Ānanda) personally saw and heard. “Thus have I heard” is the taking up of faith, proving that this sutra was truly spoken by the Buddha and that the text recorded is correct and without error. When the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa, he instructed the Venerable Ānanda: when compiling the sutras in the future, at the head of every sutra place the phrase “Thus have I heard,” to prove that it was truly spoken by the Buddha and to distinguish it from the scriptures of the outsiders. The “I” in the phrase is the compiler of the sutra, Ānanda, referring to himself. Ānanda was the Buddha’s cousin and was born on the night the Buddha attained the path. Later he left home with the Buddha and became the Buddha’s attendant, and was renowned for “never forgetting what passed his ears, foremost in much hearing.” When Ānanda left home, the Buddha had already been teaching the Dharma for twenty years; therefore he asked the Buddha to repeat for him all that had been spoken before, and Ānanda also attained the samādhi of the sovereign awareness of the nature of dharmas, so that he could comprehend all dharmas in concentration. Therefore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when the Venerable Mahākāśyapa compiled the sutra-piṭaka in the great stone cave of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered in one place and the assembly unanimously urged Ānanda to ascend the seat and recite the sutra text. In the Lotus Sutra the Buddha says: “I and Ānanda and others, at the place of the Buddha King of Emptiness, at the same time gave rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment. Ānanda always delighted in much hearing, while I always strove diligently. Therefore I have already attained supreme perfect enlightenment, while Ānanda protects and upholds my Dharma, and also protects the treasury of the Dharma of the future Buddhas, teaching and bringing to accomplishment the assembly of bodhisattvas.”

[At one time] At that time. This refers to the time when the Buddha spoke this sutra, that is, when teacher and disciple were united in the way and capacity and teaching met each other. The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma applies to gods and humans alike, and the compilation and transmission of it spread throughout the world; since the year, month and day cannot be made the same for all, “at one time” is used to record it. [Teacher and disciple] Teacher and student; master and disciple. [Capacity and teaching meeting each other] “Capacity” is the faculty of the listeners; “teaching” is the Buddha’s bestowal of teaching. Living beings’ faculties differ, and so the Buddha, according to their capacities, bestows teachings shallow or deep. “Capacity and teaching meeting each other” means that the faculties of the listeners at the dharma assembly and the Buddha’s bestowal of teaching resonate and accord. [Buddha] An abbreviation of “buddha,” here meaning Śākyamuni Buddha. “Buddha” is a Sanskrit sound, rendered into Chinese as “the Awakened One.” Inwardly awakened, he is without any deluded thoughts; outwardly awakened, he is unstained by the six dusts. [The country of Śrāvastī] Its location is in the northwest of present-day India, on the south bank of the Rapti River; its king at that time was King Prasenajit.

[Jeta] The grove of Prince Jeta. [Anāthapiṇḍada] the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada (“elder” being an honorific for a person of high virtue and great prestige). He was Sudatta, a wealthy merchant of the capital of the country of Śrāvastī. Of charitable disposition, he delighted in giving to the orphaned and the solitary (“orphan” meaning one who has lost his parents; “solitary” meaning one who has lost a spouse; “orphaned and solitary” generally referring to the poor and suffering who have no one to rely on), and so he won the fair name of “Anāthapiṇḍada,” “Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary.” [Garden] A grove or park. [The Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden] A grove in the capital of the country of Śrāvastī, where Śākyamuni Buddha spoke this sutra. The trees of this park belonged to Prince Jeta of the country of Śrāvastī, while the land belonged to the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada; the two of them jointly offered it to the Buddha, hence the name “the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden,” meaning the grove of Prince Jeta and the garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. The Buddha often preached there. The story of their joint offering of the park is this: when the Buddha was preaching in the country of Magadha, the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada of the country of Śrāvastī begged the Buddha to come to the city of Śrāvastī and convert its people, and the Buddha consented. After the Elder returned to his country, he searched everywhere for a place, and found that Prince Jeta’s grove was the most suitable for the Buddha to preach in, so he wished to buy it. The prince said in jest: “Cover the ground with gold, spread five inches thick, and it is sold.” The Elder agreed and did so. The prince, moved by the Elder’s sincerity, said: “What people prize most is nothing beyond gold and jewels. He can pour out his whole fortune to buy land and build a monastery—how am I so lacking that I cannot build one?” Thereupon he himself gave rise to the supreme intention to make an offering and asked to retract his earlier promise. The Elder would not agree, and the prince said: “You have promised to take the land for gold, but the trees were not discussed. Let the land be yours, and the grove remain mine; together let us bring the work to completion, each making his own offering.” When the Buddha came to this place, he said to Ānanda: “The park land was bought by the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada; the grove was given by Prince Jeta. The two were of one mind in jointly exalting merit. From now on, this place should be called ‘the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden.’”

[Great bhikṣus] “Bhikṣu” is the general name for one who has left home and received full ordination; males are called “bhikṣus,” females “bhikṣuṇīs.” “Great bhikṣus” are bhikṣus of lofty virtue and senior years. [Twelve hundred and fifty in number] These twelve hundred and fifty great bhikṣus were the Buddha’s constant followers. According to the Sutra of the Causes and Effects of Past and Present,

fascicle four, among these twelve hundred and fifty people were: the small group of fifty headed by Yaśas; five hundred under the teacher-and-disciples Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa; two hundred and fifty under Nadī-Kāśyapa; two hundred and fifty under Gayā-Kāśyapa; one hundred under Śāriputra; and one hundred under Mahāmaudgalyāyana. These twelve hundred and fifty people had first served the outsiders, and later, guided by the Buddha’s transformative teaching, attained the fruits; feeling the Buddha’s grace, at every dharma assembly they followed him constantly without leaving, and so were called the constant followers. Hence when the sutras list the assembly at the head of the dharma assembly, they mostly say “together with twelve hundred and fifty in number.” [Together with] In one place.

[At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged from door to door in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, arranged his seat and sat down.]

At this time the hour for the single meal of the day had come, and so the World-Honored One put on his great robe, took up his alms bowl, led his disciples with dignified and orderly deportment, and with slow steps entered the capital of the country of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city, without distinguishing between poor and lowly or rich and noble households, he received alms in order from door to door. When the begging was finished, he returned to his dwelling. The World-Honored One finished his meal, put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet clean, arranged his seat, and sat cross-legged, solemn and serene, with right mindfulness unmoving.
The translation by Yuan-Wei

Bodhiruci says: “At that time the World-Honored One, at the hour for the meal, put on his robe, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. In that city he begged in order; then he returned to his original place. When the meal was finished, he put away his robe and bowl, washed his feet, and as usual arranged his seat and sat cross-legged. He settled his body and remained, with right mindfulness unmoving.”

This passage is the particular introduction. The particular introduction is where the introductory portions of the various sutras differ from one another; it comes after the general introduction. It is also called the introduction of the arising, because it explains how that sutra’s dharma assembly came about.

The arising of this sutra’s dharma assembly is that the World-Honored One, through his daily activities (putting on his robe, holding his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even arranging his seat and sitting down), displayed through bodily teaching that prajñā is everywhere—what awakening is, and what the original scenery is.

[At that time] At this time. [World-Honored One] A venerable title of the Buddha. Because the Buddha is endowed with ten thousand virtues, is honored by the world, and is moreover supreme in the world, he is called the World-Honored One. [The hour for the meal] The hour for the single meal of the day had come. In the Sutra of Forty-Two Sections Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says: “Shaving head and beard and becoming a śramaṇa, one who receives the Dharma of the path renounces worldly goods and takes what he begs as sufficient. One meal a day, one night beneath a tree—be careful never to do more! What makes people foolish and benighted is love and desire.”

[Put on his robe] The three robes and one bowl are the possessions a bhikṣu carries with him. The three robes are the antarvāsa, the uttarāsaṅga and the saṃghāṭī; in Sanskrit all three are called kaṣāya (“kaṣāya” originally meaning a dyed, faded-color robe, because the Dharma robes worn by monks who have left home must all be dyed muddy colors). The antarvāsa is rendered into Chinese as the “body robe”; it is made of five strips (that is, five squares of cloth sewn and joined like a field, hence “field robe”), and is worn for work and for sitting and lying down. The uttarāsaṅga is worn over the antarvāsa, hence its name “upper robe”; it is made of seven strips, and is donned when performing Dharma matters and entering the assembly. The saṃghāṭī is rendered into Chinese as the “robe for the assembled multitude,” also called the great robe; it is made of nine to twenty-five strips, and is worn on solemn occasions. Now, since he was about to enter the city to beg, he deliberately put on the great robe.

[Bowl] An abbreviation of the Sanskrit pātra, the eating vessel of a bhikṣu. [The great city of Śrāvastī] The capital of the country of Śrāvastī; the Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden was five or six li southeast of the city. [Begging for food] A bhikṣu, free of all greed and seeking, subduing his pride, constantly practices begging for food to sustain his physical body and assist his work on the path. [Begging in order] In begging for food, a bhikṣu is not attached to flavor, does not slight living beings, and does not choose between rich and poor; with an equal mind he begs from house to house in order, not exceeding seven households or the prescribed time; even if his bowl is not filled, he must return. [His original place] The Jeta Grove of Anāthapiṇḍada’s Garden, where he lived. [Finished] Completed.

When the Buddha spoke other sutras, he often arose to the occasion by emitting light and displaying auspicious signs. This sutra is the Tathāgata’s mind-dharma of attaining Buddhahood, yet it arises to the occasion through daily activities—there is indeed deep meaning in this, for it shows that prajñā is nowhere else but in daily activities. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “Ordinary beings are Buddhas; affliction is bodhi. When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary being; when the following thought is awakened, one is a Buddha. When the preceding thought clings to objects, that is affliction; when the following thought leaves objects, that is bodhi.” This sutra says: “Leaving all marks—that is called all Buddhas.” The World-Honored One’s display is awareness in every thought, leaving objects in every thought; in putting on his robe and holding his bowl, entering the city to beg, and even arranging his seat and sitting down, he everywhere displays the wondrous flavor of prajñā—“not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness”—to proclaim the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā, so that the whole assembly may learn and realize within daily life what the original scenery is.

[Not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness] Not clinging to marks as real, and therefore not being moved by them. That is, not clinging to marks and not stirring the mind. [Original scenery] Also called the original face; it is a Chan expression describing the intrinsic state of the self-nature (the state of complete awakening).

There is a story about this. A woman went to ask the Buddha: how can I attain awakening? The Buddha said: what is your work? She said: I make my living by drawing water. The Buddha then told her: when you draw water, your mind should be perfectly clear and aware in every movement (do not let any unaware, habitual movement occur). The woman earnestly did as the Buddha taught, and attained awakening.

The mind should be perfectly clear and aware in every movement”—this is the wondrous method of bringing cultivation into daily life by being aware and illuminating in the present. If one can do this, one will no longer worry about having no time to cultivate, and will never again be anxious and uneasy, fearing that cultivation is being delayed. How can cultivation be brought into daily life? By never losing awareness and illumination! At all times and in all places, never losing awareness and illumination, being perfectly clear and aware of one’s own mental activity, and not being turned by circumstances.

Buddha means awakened. The Buddha is the awakened one who has already woken from the dream of ignorance; though in daily life he is the same as ordinary people, his realm is utterly different—at every moment awareness is shining forth.

The World-Honored One displayed how to cultivate within daily life: when conditions come, one gives; when conditions cease, one is still. In giving, awareness and illumination are not lost, and one is always serene and at ease—the so-called “not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness.”

In this way the World-Honored One, through daily activities such as putting on his robe, holding his bowl, begging for food, returning to his original place, eating, putting away his robe and bowl, washing his feet, and arranging his seat and sitting down, taught us that there is no time and no place where cultivation is impossible, and pointed out the point of entry for us who are people of dust and toil. Therefore in the text below, the Elder Subhūti exclaims that this is rare, and says: in doing this, the Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well!

Cultivation is divided into work on the seat and work off the seat. On the seat is training; off the seat is real combat. If one uses it well, there is no time and no place that is not cultivation. The Sixth Patriarch said: “What is called sitting in Chan? In this Dharma gate there is no obstruction and no hindrance (one is not constrained by circumstances and conditions). Externally, in regard to all good and evil circumstances, not giving rise to thought is called sitting; inwardly seeing the intrinsic nature as unmoving is called Chan.” A verse says: A day of practice earns a day of merit; a day without practice leaves a day empty. True cultivation lies in daily life; the Buddha’s path is itself within living.

There was a practitioner named Bāhiya who, after a long journey, arrived dust-covered in the city of Śrāvastī to seek the Dharma from the Buddha, and saw the Buddha in the city begging for alms from house to house, his every gesture and movement graceful and beautiful, his six faculties fully tamed and guarded, serene and still. Bāhiya came forward, bowed, and asked the Buddha to teach him the Dharma, to teach him the Dharma of endless benefit and peace. The Buddha said that he was now going from door to door for alms and it was not suitable to teach the Dharma. But Bāhiya begged again and again, and so the Buddha taught him on the spot: Bāhiya! You should train thus: in the seen there is only the seen; in the heard there is only the heard; in the known there is only the known; in the cognized there is only the cognized. Bāhiya! When you can make it so that in the seen there is only the seen, in the heard there is only the heard, in the known there is only the known, and in the cognized there is only the cognized, then you have reached the state of no clinging and no obstruction. If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world, and no future world either. Since you have neither this present world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed. (The original text is found in the Pali Udāna, chapter one, section ten.)

[The three times] The past world, the present world and the future world. Dharmas that have already arisen and ceased are called “the past world”; dharmas that have arisen and not yet ceased are called “the present world”; dharmas not yet arisen and not yet produced are called “the future world.”

Note: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no present world, and no future world either. Since you have neither this present world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed.” It would seem it should be: “If you have no clinging and no obstruction, then you have no past world, and no future world either. Since you have neither the past world nor the future world, all sorrow, lamentation, pain and grief are utterly dispersed.” This may be a mistake in the copying of the text.
Subhūti” is the Chinese rendering of the name of Subhūti. Subhūti rose from his seat and requested the World-Honored One to teach the Dharma. From this section on, the sutra enters the main part.

[At that time the Elder Subhūti rose from his seat in the midst of the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha: Rare indeed, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well. World-Honored One! When good men and good women give rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment, how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?]

At this time the Elder Subhūti, in the midst of the great assembly, rose from his seat. Baring his right shoulder, placing his right knee on the ground, joining his palms in reverence, he said to the Buddha: Incomparably wondrous, World-Honored One! Taking your own person as the model, you teach thus by bodily example at all times and in all places—this is truly the best protection and care and the best instructive guidance for all bodhisattvas! World-Honored One! When good men and good women who have given rise to the great mind of becoming Buddha and liberating living beings—how should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?

How should they abide? How should they subdue their minds?”—this is the main theme of this sutra. The first part of the sutra answers these two questions; at the beginning of the second part (Section Seventeen: Ultimately No Self), Subhūti raises these two questions again, and the World-Honored One answers them further.
For whom was the Diamond Sutra spoken? From this passage it can be known that the Buddha spoke this sutra for ordinary beings who have given rise to the great mind.

[At that time] At this time, that is, when the World-Honored One had finished sitting at ease. [Elder] A bhikṣu of advanced years, virtue and prestige. [Subhūti] One of the Buddha’s ten great disciples; rendered into Chinese as Kongsheng, Shanjian and Shanji, and renowned among the ten great disciples as “foremost in understanding emptiness.” [Baring his right shoulder] When wearing the kaṣāya robe, to bare the right shoulder and cover the left. This was originally a ceremony of respect in ancient India, and Buddhism followed it: when a bhikṣu paid respects to the Buddha or inquired of his teacher or the saṃgha, he had to bare the right shoulder, meaning that he was ready to serve and to receive orders and be sent on errands. [Said] To state something to a superior. [Rare indeed] Incomparably wondrous! An expression of praise. [Tathāgata] One of the ten titles of the Buddha. Usually “World-Honored One” is the general title, used in addressing him; “Buddha” indicates the virtue of fruition; “Tathāgata” indicates the virtue of nature.
[The Buddha’s ten titles]

The Buddha has ten venerable titles: 1. Tathāgata—the Buddha rides the way of suchness, comes to accomplish perfect enlightenment, and comes to the three realms to bestow transformation. 2. Arhat (worthy of offerings)—the Buddha is worthy of the offerings of gods and humans. 3. Fully Enlightened—the Buddha truly and universally knows all dharmas. 4. Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct—the Buddha is complete in the three knowledges of the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye and the extinction of taints, and in the five practices of the noble practice, the brahma practice, the divine practice, the infant practice and the sick practice. 5. Well-Gone—the Buddha freely and well departs into nirvāṇa. 6. Knower of the World—the Buddha can understand the affairs and principles of all worlds. 7. Unsurpassed One—the Buddha is the being supreme beyond all. 8. Tamer of Beings—the Buddha is the great being who tames and governs all living beings, causing them to leave defilement and attain nirvāṇa. 9. Teacher of Gods and Humans—the Buddha is the guide of all gods and humans. 10. World-Honored One—the Buddha is the one honored in common by all the world.

[The Tathāgata truly protects and cares for the bodhisattvas well, and truly entrusts and instructs the bodhisattvas well.] “Protects and cares” means to tend, protect and compassionately remember. “Entrusts and instructs” means to entrust, charge and admonish, which also means to teach. This passage is Subhūti’s incomparable praise of the World-Honored One for taking his own person as the model and tending, protecting, guiding and teaching the bodhisattvas at all times and in all places. [Good men and good women] Men and women who observe the five precepts and the ten good deeds. [Supreme perfect enlightenment] Perfect and supreme wisdom—the wisdom of the Buddha. Rendered into Chinese as “supreme, correct and universal enlightenment,” also called “supreme universal knowledge.” [Giving rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment] Giving rise to the great mind of becoming Buddha. “Giving rise to the mind of supreme perfect enlightenment” is also abbreviated as “giving rise to the bodhi mind.” Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna says in the Great Treatise on the Perfection of Wisdom,

fascicle forty-one: “When a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind, taking the supreme way as his condition—‘I shall become Buddha’—this is called the bodhi mind.” [How] In what way. “How” has the following several meanings: for what reason, why; in what way, what to do, how it is. [How should they abide?] “How should they abide” means “how should one abide”; this uses inverted sentence order, placing “should” after “how” in order to strengthen the tone. (The answer to “How should they abide?” is in section four: “giving without abiding in marks.” Not abiding in marks is emptiness, and giving is compassion; compassion and emptiness cultivated together—this is the bodhisattva path.) [How should they subdue their minds?] How should they subdue their minds? (The answer is in section three: single-mindedly liberating all living beings while being without the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of living beings and the mark of a life-span. This is the wondrous remedy for affliction: as it is said, to stop water from boiling by ladling it out is not as good as withdrawing the firewood from beneath the cauldron. To single-mindedly liberate all living beings while being without the four marks—this too is compassion and emptiness cultivated together.) [Inversion] A rhetorical figure that inverts word order to strengthen the tone, harmonize rhythm or interweave sentence patterns; it was constantly used in ancient Chinese, so one should be attentive to this when reading Buddhist sutras.

Day after day the World-Honored One displayed thus (not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness), yet the great assembly did not notice; today it was at last seen through by Subhūti, foremost in understanding emptiness (who saw the signs), personally perceiving the Tathāgata’s painstaking care, and he praised him without cease. When the World-Honored One had sat at ease, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and said to the Buddha: Incomparably wondrous, World-Honored One! Taking your own person as the model, not grasping at marks and unmoving in suchness, you teach thus by bodily example at all times and in all places—this is truly the best protection and care and the best instructive guidance for all bodhisattvas!

But why are the bodhisattvas unable to achieve “not grasping at marks, unmoving in suchness”? For this reason Subhūti asked the World-Honored One: how should they abide, and how should they subdue their minds?

By the Buddha’s original vow, he wished only to lay bare the truth completely (to set out whole the truth of life and the universe), so that everyone might become Buddha. But living beings are thin in virtue and heavy in defilement, weak in will, unable to bear it, and hard to address plainly (just as in section fourteen of this sutra the Buddha says: “If again there is a person who, hearing this sutra, is not startled, not frightened and not afraid, know that such a person is most rare.” And as at the Lotus assembly, when Śāriputra three times begged the World-Honored One to reveal the foremost, rare and hard-to-understand Dharma, and when the World-Honored One began to expound it, five thousand bhikṣus refused to hear and withdrew from the assembly). So he had no choice but to use secret and skillful means and accommodate them; hence the word “well.”

Day after day the World-Honored One displayed thus; this is truly the most skillful protection and care and the most skillful entrusting and instructing of the bodhisattvas. As it is said: not by verbal teaching, but by turning them through his own person—the painstaking care of a good craftsman.

In the sutra text of this section, “How should they abide?” has two readings: the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular editions adopt “How should they abide?” while another reading, based on Tang dynasty manuscripts and Ming dynasty block-printed editions, proposes that this passage should be “How should one abide?” Is it “How should they abide” or “How should one abide”? This book follows the Qianlong Tripitaka and the popular editions in adopting “How should they abide?”

The reason is this: “How should they abide” in fact means “how should one abide”; it is only that, to strengthen the tone, inverted sentence order is used, placing “should” after “how.” Inversion is very common in rhetoric, used to strengthen the tone and make the words vivid. For example, in “The Foolish Old Man Removes the Mountains” in the Liezi,

“How great is your lack of sense!” means: your lack of sense (hui, interchangeable with “wisdom”) is great! And Wei Zheng’s “Expressing My Feelings,” “On ancient trees cold birds cry; in empty mountains night apes wail,” means: on ancient trees cold birds cry, in empty mountains night apes wail. In fact, the four characters “Thus have I heard” at the very beginning of the sutra are also an inversion. If it were rendered as “I heard thus,” not only would the force of the wording and the beauty of the style be much diminished, but the poetic realm would be as different as heaven and earth.
Question: Why is “How should they abide?” explained as “how should they abide and uphold?”

Answer: Master Kumarajiva’s rendering “How should they abide” is excellent; the word “abide” fits perfectly with the sutra text before and after it. (For example, the last line of section four: “Subhūti! A bodhisattva should simply abide as he is taught.”) But the meaning of “abide” here needs to be correctly interpreted. What cultivators care about most is three questions: how to abide in the mind (to gather the mind in and not let it scatter), how to practice (to correct one’s actual conduct of body, speech and mind), and how to subdue the mind. Judging from several other translations, in the Sanskrit original Subhūti raised these three questions. For example, Master Xuanzang’s translation: “World-Honored One! Those who have set out on the bodhisattva vehicle—how should they abide? How should they practice? How should they subdue their minds?” Therefore some venerable ones have criticized Master Kumarajiva’s translation as “missing one of the three questions.”

In fact, combining two questions into one (merging “how to abide in the mind” and “how to practice” into “how should they abide”) was also Master Kumarajiva’s painstaking care. The World-Honored One answered the first two questions together in “Section Four: Wondrous Practice Without Abiding” (how should one abide in the mind? how should one practice?), and then in section ten he further clarified the question of how to abide in the mind and how to practice: “Bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind abiding in form, nor give rise to a mind abiding in sound, scent, taste, touch or dharmas; they should give rise to the mind that abides nowhere.” Therefore the Master merged these two questions into one, “how should they abide,” so that the wording echoes before and after, is polished and easy on the tongue, and the reader, from the sutra text before and after, can readily grasp that this “abide” contains both the sense of abiding in the mind and that of practicing—that is, how to abide and uphold.
